hook.text: Keys guard the links between your tables. But what guards what goes INTO them?

bad.text: Say a product gets saved at minus three dollars. That's not a sale... that's a mistake.

app.text: Your app could catch that. But a database rarely has just one writer.

writers.text: The web app, the mobile app, a nightly import, someone typing queries by hand. Each one has to remember the rule.

forgets.text: And it only takes one that forgets.

schema.text: So put the rule in the schema. That's a constraint: a rule the database checks on every write, whoever's writing.

reject.text: Price has to be zero or more. Try minus three... and Postgres refuses, naming the rule you broke.

stored.text: The bad row never lands. The notebook's still the only product.

door.text: That error isn't a failure. It's the mistake caught at the door, while it's still cheap to fix.

types-in.text: And every column has a rule before you add a single one.

type.text: Its type. Say quantity is an integer, and someone sends the word many.

nan.text: Refused. It isn't too big, or too small... it just isn't a number.

domain.text: A type decides which values can exist at all. So pick it from what the value means.

money-in.text: And for money, that choice matters more than you'd think.

money.text: Add ten cents and twenty cents as floats, then ask Postgres if that's thirty cents.

false.text: False! A float is approximate, so you get point three, a long run of zeros, and a four.

exact.text: Numeric is exact, so there the answer's true. That's the honest type for a price.

null-in.text: So the value's the right kind. But does it have to be there at all?

null.text: In a database, a missing value is null. Not zero, not an empty string... no value at all.

ask.text: So for every column, ask: does every row have to know this?

default.text: An account's status has a safe fallback, so it gets a default. Leave it out, and the row comes back active.

email.text: But an account with no email makes no sense. So email is marked not null, and an insert without one is refused.

unique-in.text: Now every account has an email. But could two of them share one?

unique.text: Ada signs up. Then a second account tries her email, with a new username.

dup.text: Duplicate key, refused. One email, one account.

many.text: The primary key already keeps rows distinct. Unique guards everything else that can't repeat.

pair.text: A student takes many courses, and a course has many students. So both IDs repeat... but each pair only once.

again.text: Enroll student one in course ten a second time, and it bounces.

oneone.text: Put unique on a foreign key, and each user gets at most one profile. That's one to one.

check-in.text: That covers missing and repeated. What about values that are just wrong?

check.text: That's a check: a true or false test that every row has to pass. Price zero or more was one.

banana.text: Status has to be draft, active, or archived. So banana? Nope.

dates.text: It can compare columns, too. An event can't end before it starts, so this backwards conference never gets in.

unknown.text: One catch, though. A check only refuses false. Leave the price out, and the test comes back unknown... so the row slips through.

layers.text: That's why a required price gets three rules. Numeric for its type, a check for its range, and not null, so it's actually there.

limits.text: But some mistakes pass every rule.

twice.text: Copy a customer's email onto every one of her orders, then update just one.

valid.text: Every value is valid... and the table now gives Ada TWO emails.

next.text: Constraints stop bad values, not bad structure. One fact stored twice can still disagree with itself.
